title: Unique ID Generator Design
description: Design a distributed unique ID generator that produces sortable, collision-free identifiers across multiple data centers and services.

data.text: Unique ID generators produce identifiers that never collide, even across thousands of independent services. They appear in almost every system: user IDs, order IDs, message IDs, and payment transaction IDs. In interviews, ID generator design tests your ability to reason about uniqueness guarantees, sortability, time-based ordering, and coordination in distributed environments.

Auto-incrementing database columns are simple but create a single point of failure. Scaling the database shards the sequence and requires coordination between shards. Database sequences also leak information about total records and growth rate. For distributed systems, a centralized sequence does not scale horizontally and introduces coupling between services that should be independent.

UUIDs are 128-bit random or pseudo-random identifiers that guarantee an astronomically low collision probability without coordination. Version 4 UUIDs use random numbers and never require a central generator. However, UUIDs are not sortable by creation time because the timestamp portion is not at the most significant bits. Random UUIDs also cause B-tree index fragmentation in databases, slowing down range queries and inserts.

Snowflake encodes a 64-bit integer from five components: 1 bit for sign, 41 bits for a custom epoch millisecond timestamp, 10 bits for a worker or machine ID, and 12 bits for a per-machine sequence number. The worker ID must be unique within the deployment and is typically assigned via ZooKeeper, etcd, or a configuration management system. Within the same millisecond, the sequence number increments to avoid collisions on the same machine.

data.caption: Bit layout of a Snowflake ID
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[64-bit ID] --> B[1 bit: Sign]
    A --> C[41 bits: Timestamp]
    A --> D[10 bits: Worker ID]
    A --> E[12 bits: Sequence]
    C --> F[Custom epoch]
    D --> G[Up to 1024 workers]
    E --> H[4096 IDs per ms per worker]

data.text: For services that already depend on a relational database, the ticket approach pre-allocates blocks of IDs from a centralized table. Each service instance requests a block of 1,000 IDs and uses them locally without further coordination. When the block is exhausted, the service requests a new block. This approach reduces database round trips while maintaining uniqueness through the source of truth.

data.title: Clock synchronization
data.text: Time-based ID generators require NTP or a similar clock synchronization protocol. Monitor clock drift and failover to UUID generation if the clock drifts beyond a safe threshold.

items.text: IDs must be globally unique with an astronomically low collision probability
items.hint: Collisions corrupt data and break referential integrity

items.text: IDs should be sortable by creation time for efficient range queries
items.hint: Time-based IDs avoid expensive ORDER BY DESC operations

items.text: Generator must scale horizontally without coordination overhead
items.hint: New instances should start generating IDs immediately

items.text: Generator should tolerate clock skew and failover gracefully
items.hint: Use NTP monitoring and fallback strategies

terms.definition: A 64-bit distributed ID format that encodes a timestamp, worker ID, and sequence number for sortable, collision-free identifiers.
A unique numeric identifier assigned to each instance in a Snowflake deployment so IDs generated on different machines do not collide.
The difference in time between two machines; time-based ID generators require clocks to stay synchronized.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: UUID v4 is simple and portable but not time-sortable and causes index fragmentation
Snowflake produces 64-bit, time-ordered IDs without coordination after initialization
Worker IDs must be unique and can be assigned via ZooKeeper or configuration management
Pre-allocate ID blocks when using a database as the sequence source of truth
Monitor clock drift and fall back to random IDs if synchronization fails
data.takeaway: A well-designed ID generator removes coordination overhead while delivering sortable, unique identifiers at scale.

items.question: Should IDs be sequential?
items.answer: Sequential IDs are easy to read but leak information about volume and timing. Sortable IDs are usually sufficient for ordering without revealing sensitive business metrics.

items.question: What if two workers generate the same ID?
items.answer: A well-assigned worker ID prevents this. If a collision somehow occurs, rely on a database unique constraint and regenerate the ID automatically.

data.title: Implement a Simple ID Generator
data.description: Write a function that generates a 64-bit Snowflake-style ID given a timestamp, worker ID, and sequence number. Calculate how many unique IDs per second a single worker can generate with 12 sequence bits.
data.expectedOutcome: With 12 sequence bits, a single worker can generate 4,096 unique IDs per millisecond, or 4,096,000 IDs per second
